question: What information does iterative magnitude pruning encode in a winning-ticket mask, how does SGD use it after rewinding, and why must pruning usually proceed iteratively?

key_findings.claim: At matching sparsities, an IMP mask identifies an axis-aligned subspace that intersects the same linearly connected low-error mode as the preceding dense solution.
key_findings.evidence: The paper interpolates between successive pruning-level solutions and projected points. Zero error barriers align with whether the next sparse network is matching, motivating the interpretation of the mask as geometric information about where a desired connected sublevel set intersects a coordinate subspace.

key_findings.claim: SGD can recover the matching connected mode after substantial perturbations to a rewound, masked network.
key_findings.evidence: Perturbation experiments at rewind points show that retraining often returns to a solution linearly connected to the unperturbed matching endpoint. This robustness explains how early training can exploit mask information even when the rewound weights are not already close in Euclidean distance to the final solution.

key_findings.claim: The Hessian spectrum and distance moved by coordinate projection predict a maximum safe one-shot pruning ratio.
key_findings.evidence: A local quadratic model treats the low-error sublevel set as an ellipsoid. Its intersection threshold with a random lower-dimensional subspace depends on the spectrum: flatter directions and a shorter projection allow larger pruning steps. Empirical pruning thresholds track the resulting estimate.

key_findings.claim: Adaptive pruning based on the predicted intersection limit can reach the target sparse performance in fewer pruning rounds than fixed-ratio IMP.
key_findings.evidence: The adaptive procedure selects the largest per-level pruning fraction predicted to remain in the matching low-error set. A CIFAR-100 ResNet-18 example reaches comparable sparsity and performance in seven levels rather than the eleven used by fixed-ratio IMP.

key_findings.claim: The geometric evidence explains the tested IMP trajectories but does not establish a universal causal characterization of winning tickets.
key_findings.evidence: Connectivity, perturbation recovery, and Hessian estimates are measured on selected vision models and require costly path or curvature probes. The quadratic and random-subspace approximations can fail in nonlocal, nonsmooth, or highly anisotropic regimes, and the experiments do not cover foundation-model scale.

method.core_idea: Interpret a pruning mask as a coordinate subspace selected to preserve access to a particular connected low-error region, then use landscape geometry to explain mask utility and iterative pruning.
method.mechanism: Iterative magnitude pruning trains, removes low-magnitude coordinates, rewinds surviving weights, and retrains. The analysis compares successive solutions with linear-mode-connectivity paths, perturbs rewind points to test SGD recovery, approximates local sublevel sets with Hessian ellipsoids, and predicts how much dimensionality a projection can remove before losing intersection with the matching mode.
assumptions: Linear interpolation error is an informative proxy for membership in the same useful solution mode.
A local quadratic Hessian approximation captures enough of the relevant low-error sublevel geometry.
Coordinate projections induced by magnitude pruning can be compared with random-subspace intersection arguments.
Matching endpoint performance and the tested rewind schedule adequately represent winning-ticket trainability.

techniques.role: Produces successive masks and sparse matching solutions whose geometry is analyzed.
Tests whether adjacent pruning-level solutions occupy a shared zero-barrier error mode.
Measures whether SGD robustly returns to the matching connected mode.
Approximates sublevel-set flatness and the dimensional threshold for safe projection.
Chooses a per-round pruning fraction from the predicted intersection limit.

evaluations.setting: CIFAR-10 with ResNet-20, CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18, and ImageNet with ResNet-50 under IMP and weight or learning-rate rewinding.
evaluations.metric: Matching accuracy, sparsity, and maximum loss/error barrier along interpolation paths between pruning levels.
evaluations.result: Zero-barrier connectivity between successive pruned solutions is strongly associated with whether the new subnetwork remains matching at high sparsity.
evaluations.baseline: Nonmatching pruning levels, earlier rewind points, and dense or preceding-level solutions.

evaluations.setting: Masked rewind points subjected to controlled weight perturbations before retraining.
evaluations.metric: Endpoint accuracy and linear connectivity to the unperturbed matching solution.
evaluations.result: Across the tested regimes, SGD often recovers a matching endpoint in the same connected mode despite large early perturbations.
evaluations.baseline: Unperturbed retraining and rewind points that do not produce matching subnetworks.

evaluations.setting: Per-level Hessian-spectrum analysis and adaptive pruning on image-classification networks.
evaluations.metric: Predicted versus observed safe pruning fraction and number of pruning rounds to target sparsity.
evaluations.result: The curvature-based threshold follows the observed limit, and the CIFAR-100 adaptive example needs seven rounds versus eleven fixed-ratio rounds at comparable final performance.

limitations: The empirical study is confined to image classification and ResNet-family architectures rather than language models or structurally different networks.
Full or density-estimated Hessian spectra and connectivity sweeps are expensive enough to weaken the practical advantage of adaptive pruning.
A local ellipsoidal approximation need not describe the nonlocal route SGD follows through a nonlinear loss landscape.
Linear connectivity is evidence of shared geometry, not a complete causal account of why a mask generalizes.
Matching final accuracy does not measure calibration, robustness, fairness, or transfer of the sparse model.
failure_modes: A mask can project outside the useful connected sublevel set when a pruning step is too aggressive.
Magnitude coordinates may not align with flat directions in architectures or training regimes unlike those tested.
A noisy Hessian estimate can recommend an unsafe pruning ratio.
SGD may fail to return to the desired mode when rewinding is too early or the sparse optimization basin is unstable.
reusable_insights: Treat a sparsity mask as geometric information about an allowable coordinate subspace, not merely as a list of expendable weights.
Audit pruning transitions with both endpoint accuracy and path connectivity to detect loss of a useful mode.
Choose pruning step size adaptively from curvature and projection distance rather than assume one fixed fraction is safe everywhere.
Retraining creates a new population of small weights, explaining why repeated prune-retrain cycles can outperform one-shot pruning.
open_questions: Can cheap curvature sketches or online probes replace full Hessian-spectrum estimates for adaptive pruning?
Does the mask-as-intersecting-subspace account hold for transformers, mixture-of-experts models, and structured pruning?
Which geometric diagnostic predicts transfer and robustness of a ticket, not only matching in-distribution accuracy?
Can a training objective deliberately shape flat coordinate-aligned directions so that one-shot pruning succeeds?

competitive_landscape.title: The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis: Finding Sparse, Trainable Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Introduces winning tickets and iterative magnitude pruning as sparse subnetworks that can train to dense-network performance from selected initial weights.
competitive_landscape.difference: The original work establishes the phenomenon and algorithm; this paper asks what the learned mask conveys after rewinding and answers through connected-sublevel-set geometry.

competitive_landscape.title: Stabilizing the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis
competitive_landscape.relationship: Shows that rewinding to early training can make tickets stable and trainable in deeper networks and larger-scale settings.
competitive_landscape.difference: It identifies rewind timing and optimization stability as practical conditions; this paper attributes mask utility and per-round pruning limits to error-landscape geometry and curvature.

competitive_landscape.title: Linear Mode Connectivity and the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis
competitive_landscape.relationship: Uses linear mode connectivity to relate SGD stability and rewind points to successful lottery tickets.
competitive_landscape.difference: That work connects ticket stability to SGD noise and rewind time; this paper focuses on what the mask itself encodes, links pruning dimension to Hessian spectra, and derives an adaptive pruning rule.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: A winning-ticket mask encodes the coordinate subspace intersecting a matching connected low-error mode, while curvature controls how much can be safely pruned at each IMP round.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Connectivity, rewind perturbation, Hessian-spectrum, magnitude-direction, and adaptive-pruning experiments support the account across three ResNet/image-dataset settings.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The paper offers a coherent geometric synthesis and an actionable pruning heuristic, but its expensive local diagnostics and limited architecture scope leave universality unproven.
